paper_metadata.title: Achieving high strength and high conductivity synergy through cryogenic deformation and aging treatment

evidence.quote: In order to achieve high strength and high conductivity of typical precipitation-strengthened CuCrZr alloys, the combination of plastic deformation (rolling at room and cryogenic temperatures) and aging treatment was applied in this study
In CuCrZr alloys, the electrical conductivity is usually determined by the composition of the alloying elements and their microstructure

A small fraction of the precipitates is identified as fcc Cr phases (Figs. 8b–1), while the majority are ordered fcc Cr-rich phases (Figs. 8b–2).

The appearance of superlattice diffraction spots in the FFT image of Figs. 8b–2 indicates that some Cr atoms in the initially formed fcc Cr phases have been replaced by Cu atoms as the aging time increases, resulting in the formation of ordered fcc Cr-rich phases

attributes.size: exceeding 1 μm in length, widths of several hundred nanometers

evidence.quote: Most of these micron-sized Cr phases appear elongated 'rice-grain' morphology along the rolling direction, with lengths exceeding 1 μm and widths of several hundred nanometers. ... High resolution TEM (HRTEM) images and corresponding fast fourier transform (FFT) images (Fig. 7b) identify these precipitates as bcc Cr phases.

Moreover, the Zr-rich phases (~200 nm in size) are observed adjacent to the Cr phases (Fig. 7d–f), and show a morphology similar to that of the Cr phases, which suggests that the Zr-rich phase also formed during the solution process.

attributes.location: within T/M lamellae and elongated grains

attributes.size: average width of twin/matrix (T/M) lamellae about 18.6 nm; thinnest twin 4 nm

evidence.quote: A considerable number of grains of nanoscale deformation twins exist in the CTRA sample (Fig. 6b–d), indicating that cryogenic deformation promotes twinning formation, in consistent with the EBSD results in Fig. 5. The twin lamellae in the CTRA sample are relatively narrow and difficult to distinguish from the matrix. Through statistical analysis, the average width of twin/matrix (T/M) lamellae is about 18.6 nm and a volume fraction of 4%, while that of the thinnest twin is only 4 nm.
